passed.title: Comparisons against null yield null, so `filter` silently drops those rows
passed.trap: `DataFrame.filter` keeps only rows where the predicate is True. A comparison with a null value gives null, not True or False, so the row is discarded. Pandas users expect `col != 'ok'` to keep missing values, because NaN != 'ok' is True there; in Polars those rows vanish without any warning. Use `Expr.ne_missing` / `Expr.eq_missing`, or add an explicit `| pl.col(...).is_null()` when nulls should be kept.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "status": ["ok", None, "bad"]})

# Habit: "everything that is not ok" -- the null row is silently dropped
wrong = df.filter(pl.col("status") != "ok")
print(wrong["id"].to_list())  # [3]

# Null-aware comparison keeps the missing status
right = df.filter(pl.col("status").ne_missing("ok"))
print(right["id"].to_list())  # [2, 3]

# Equivalent explicit form
also = df.filter((pl.col("status") != "ok") | pl.col("status").is_null())
print(also["id"].to_list())  # [2, 3]

passed.title: NaN and null are different values: the null methods ignore NaN and the NaN methods ignore null
passed.trap: In pandas, NaN is the missing-value marker, so `dropna`/`fillna` remove it. In Polars, missing data is null. NaN is an ordinary floating-point value. `DataFrame.drop_nulls` and `DataFrame.fill_null` leave NaN untouched, and `DataFrame.fill_nan` leaves nulls untouched. To handle both, convert NaN to null first with `fill_nan(None)`, then apply the null method.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": [1.0, float("nan"), None]})

# drop_nulls keeps the NaN row
print(df.drop_nulls()["x"].to_list())  # [1.0, nan]

# fill_null does not touch NaN, and fill_nan does not touch null
print(df.fill_null(0.0)["x"].to_list())  # [1.0, nan, 0.0]
print(df.fill_nan(0.0)["x"].to_list())   # [1.0, 0.0, None]

# Treat both as missing: NaN -> null, then fill nulls
print(df.fill_nan(None).fill_null(0.0)["x"].to_list())  # [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]

passed.title: `group_by` output order is not guaranteed unless you ask for it
passed.trap: Pandas `groupby` sorts the group keys by default, but `DataFrame.group_by` does not guarantee any group order. Code that takes the first row or zips the result against another list can therefore silently misalign. Pass `maintain_order=True` to get groups in input (first-appearance) order, which is slower and blocks the streaming engine, or call `.sort(...)` on the result. The order of rows within each group is always preserved, regardless of `maintain_order`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"k": ["b", "a", "b", "c"], "v": [1, 2, 3, 4]})

# Default df.group_by("k") gives groups in arbitrary order -- do not rely on it

# Order of first appearance
ordered = df.group_by("k", maintain_order=True).agg(pl.col("v").sum())
print(ordered.rows())  # [('b', 4), ('a', 2), ('c', 4)]

# Pandas-like sorted keys: sort explicitly
sorted_out = df.group_by("k").agg(pl.col("v").sum()).sort("k")
print(sorted_out.rows())  # [('a', 2), ('b', 4), ('c', 4)]

passed.title: Most methods return a new frame, but `extend` and `drop_in_place` mutate the original
passed.trap: `DataFrame.drop` returns a new frame, so calling it without reassigning the result has no effect. Some methods do mutate the frame. `DataFrame.drop_in_place` removes the column from the frame and returns it as a Series. `DataFrame.extend` appends to the frame's own memory and returns the frame only for convenience. To keep the original unchanged, call `extend` on a `DataFrame.clone()`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
df.drop("b")  # result discarded: df is unchanged
print(df.columns)  # ['a', 'b']

s = df.drop_in_place("b")  # mutates df and returns the Series
print(s.name, df.columns)  # b ['a']

df1 = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
df2 = pl.DataFrame({"a": [3]})
combined = df1.clone().extend(df2)  # df1 untouched
print(df1.height, combined.height)  # 2 3

df1.extend(df2)  # mutates df1 in place
print(df1.height)  # 3

passed.title: `bottom_k` skips nulls and returns unordered rows; `sort().head()` puts nulls first
passed.trap: `DataFrame.bottom_k` always prefers non-null values, even with `reverse=True`. Its output is not guaranteed to be in any order, so call `.sort(...)` afterwards if order matters. `sort(...).head(k)` is not equivalent, because an ascending sort puts nulls first by default, so the null rows come out as the "smallest". The old `descending` parameter was renamed `reverse` in 1.0.0.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"name": ["a", "b", "c", "d"], "score": [3, None, 1, 2]})

# sort + head: the null row counts as the smallest
print(df.sort("score").head(2).rows())  # [('b', None), ('c', 1)]

# bottom_k ignores nulls; sort the result because its order is unspecified
print(df.bottom_k(2, by="score").sort("score").rows())  # [('c', 1), ('d', 2)]

# reverse=True (formerly descending) gives the largest values, still no nulls
print(df.bottom_k(2, by="score", reverse=True).sort("score").rows())  # [('d', 2), ('a', 3)]

passed.title: `cast` is strict by default, and `strict=False` silently turns bad values into nulls
passed.trap: `DataFrame.cast` defaults to `strict=True`, so a single unparsable string or out-of-range value makes the whole cast raise an error. With `strict=False`, the cast succeeds and every invalid value becomes null without any warning. This can quietly corrupt aggregates later. If you use `strict=False`, check `Series.null_count` afterwards to see how many values were lost.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"x": ["1", "2", "oops"]})

try:
    df.cast({"x": pl.Int64})
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))

lenient = df.cast({"x": pl.Int64}, strict=False)
print(lenient["x"].to_list())     # [1, 2, None]
print(lenient["x"].null_count())  # 1 value silently lost

passed.title: `drop` raises on missing columns unless `strict=False`
passed.trap: By default, `DataFrame.drop` checks that every named column exists and raises an error if any is missing. Defensive cleanup code such as "drop these columns if present" therefore fails on frames that lack one of them. Pass `strict=False` to ignore names that are not in the schema.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1], "b": [2]})

try:
    df.drop("b", "c")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))

print(df.drop("b", "c", strict=False).columns)  # ['a']

passed.title: `DataFrame.approx_n_unique` is deprecated and only approximate
passed.trap: `DataFrame.approx_n_unique` has been deprecated since 0.20.11 and emits a deprecation warning. Replace it with `DataFrame.select` combined with `Expr.approx_n_unique`, for example `df.select(pl.all().approx_n_unique())`. That method uses HyperLogLog++, so its result is an estimate. When you need an exact distinct count per column, use `Expr.n_unique` instead.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 3, 4], "b": [1, 2, 1, 1]})

# Replacement for the deprecated df.approx_n_unique()
approx = df.select(pl.all().approx_n_unique())
print(approx.to_dicts())

# Exact distinct counts per column
exact = df.select(pl.all().n_unique())
print(exact.to_dicts())  # [{'a': 4, 'b': 2}]
